prompt: With only `orders_placed_at_idx`, why was `count(*)` an index-only scan and `sum(total_cents)` not?
hint: Which columns does each query touch?

choices.text: sum() is not allowed in an index-only scan
choices.why: Any aggregate is; the issue is that total_cents is not in the index.

choices.text: total_cents is not in the index
choices.why: Right: count(*) needed no column, sum needed one the index lacks.

choices.text: The second query ran on a cold cache
choices.why: It found all its pages in memory; the plan type was different.

choices.text: count(*) is answered from pg_class.reltuples without reading the index
choices.why: It read 299 index pages; reltuples is only an estimate.

prompt: A plan says `Index Only Scan` with `Heap Fetches: 87062` out of 107,780 rows. How should you read it?
hint: The name promises; the number reports.

choices.text: As an index-only scan working normally
choices.why: Most rows went to the table, which is what the name says it avoids.

choices.text: As an error: the index is corrupt
choices.why: Nothing is corrupt; the visibility map was cleared by an update.

choices.text: As mostly an ordinary index scan
choices.why: Right: 87,265 page accesses against 299 when the map was clean.

choices.text: As a sign the planner should have chosen a sequential scan
choices.why: Maybe, but the first reading is that the visibility map is stale; a VACUUM brought it to 0.

prompt: Why can an index-only scan not simply trust every index entry?
hint: What is written in the row's header, not in the index?

choices.text: Index entries hold only part of each value
choices.why: A B-tree entry holds the whole key; the issue is visibility.

choices.text: The index cannot say if the row is visible to you
choices.why: Right: an entry may point at a deleted or uncommitted row.

choices.text: Index entries are only updated when VACUUM runs
choices.why: Inserts and non-HOT updates add entries immediately.

choices.text: The index is sorted, so it may return rows in the wrong order
choices.why: Order is what an index gets right; visibility is what it cannot know.

prompt: What sets a page's bit in the visibility map, and what clears it?

choices.text: VACUUM sets it; a row change clears it
choices.why: Right: and that is why one UPDATE cost 87,062 heap fetches.

choices.text: ANALYZE sets it; VACUUM clears it
choices.why: VACUUM is what sets it; ANALYZE only samples.

choices.text: Index builds set it; SELECTs clear it
choices.why: Reading never clears it, and building an index does not set it.

choices.text: A checkpoint sets it; a restart clears it
choices.why: The map survives restarts; writes to rows clear it.

prompt: Right after the UPDATE of 43,422 rows, `relallvisible` still showed 16,667 of 16,667. Why?

choices.text: Updates of status never touch the visibility map
choices.why: The next scan showed 87,062 heap fetches: the map had changed.

choices.text: The UPDATE was not committed yet
choices.why: psql runs it in autocommit; it was committed.

choices.text: pg_class holds the count from the last VACUUM
choices.why: Right: after VACUUM it read 17,029 of 17,029.

choices.text: The map only covers pages written by market.sql
choices.why: It covers every page; VACUUM marked the new ones too.

prompt: The UPDATE changed 43,422 rows and the next index-only scan made 87,062 heap fetches. Roughly how many index entries per updated row does that point to?
A dashboard's index-only scan over today's events is fast at 6 a.m. and slow by noon, with `Heap Fetches` climbing all morning. What is the likely cause and remedy?

choices.text: The index is bloated; REINDEX it every hour
choices.why: Heap Fetches count table visits, which a rebuilt index does not avoid.

choices.text: Today's pages lose their bits; vacuum them sooner
choices.why: Right: the query asks about exactly the pages being written, so autovacuum must keep up there.

choices.text: Statistics are stale; run ANALYZE
choices.why: ANALYZE does not set visibility bits.

choices.text: The cache went cold; add memory
choices.why: Heap Fetches count visits whether the page is in memory or not.

prompt: In `CREATE INDEX … ON orders (customer_id, placed_at) INCLUDE (id, status, total_cents)`, what can the INCLUDE columns do?
hint: They live only in the leaf entries.

choices.text: Be searched with = like the key
choices.why: Only key columns can be searched.

choices.text: Sort the results when no key is given
choices.why: The tree is ordered by its key alone.

choices.text: Be read, so the query needs no table
choices.why: Right: they are there to be returned.

choices.text: Enforce uniqueness together with the key
choices.why: They never take part in uniqueness, which is one of their uses.

prompt: The first index, `(customer_id, placed_at) INCLUDE (status, total_cents)`, removed the Sort but still read the table. What was missing?

choices.text: A VACUUM after building the index
choices.why: The map was clean; the plan was not even an index-only scan.

choices.text: placed_at DESC in the key
choices.why: The scan ran backward and gave the order without it.

choices.text: The id column
choices.why: Right: the query returns id, and one missing column sends every row to the heap.

choices.text: An ANALYZE so the planner trusted it
choices.why: The planner used it; it just could not answer from it alone.

prompt: Why must `placed_at` be a key column rather than in `INCLUDE` for the customer-orders query?
hint: The query has ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 10.

choices.text: INCLUDE cannot hold timestamps
choices.why: INCLUDE holds any type.

choices.text: Only key columns put rows in order
choices.why: Right: in INCLUDE the rows would come in no order and need a sort.

choices.text: Key columns are cheaper to store
choices.why: They are copied into upper levels too, so if anything they cost more.

choices.text: placed_at is in the WHERE
choices.why: It is in the ORDER BY; the WHERE is on customer_id.

prompt: You need `email` unique in `customers` and want `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE email = …` to be index-only. Which index fits?

choices.text: UNIQUE (email, name)
choices.why: Only the pair would be unique, so two rows could share an email.

choices.text: UNIQUE (email) INCLUDE (name)
choices.why: Right: email stays unique and name is carried to be read.

choices.text: A hash index on email with INCLUDE (name)
choices.why: Hash indexes support neither UNIQUE nor INCLUDE.

choices.text: Two indexes: UNIQUE (email) and one on name
choices.why: An index on name does not help a lookup by email.

prompt: Columns that a query only returns, and never searches or sorts on, go after the key in an ___ clause.
hint: The keyword that comes after the parentheses.

prompt: After the covering index, HOT updates of `orders` went from 49,051 of 49,119 to 0 of 51,946. Why?

choices.text: The covering index made the pages fuller
choices.why: An index lives in its own file; the table's pages did not change.

choices.text: total_cents became an indexed column
choices.why: Right: an update that changes an indexed value cannot be HOT.

choices.text: pgbench ran with more clients the second time
choices.why: Both runs used -c 8 -j 4 -T 15.

choices.text: The statistics counters were not reset
choices.why: They were reset before each run with pg_stat_reset_single_table_counters.

prompt: Throughput was 3275 transactions a second without the covering index and 3461 with it. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: Compare a timing with a counter.

choices.text: That the covering index speeds up writes
choices.why: Nothing in it can make a write cheaper; the gap is noise.

choices.text: That indexes have no write cost on this machine
choices.why: The HOT counter shows every update now writes five index entries.

choices.text: That the run should be repeated until the numbers agree
choices.why: Repeating helps a timing; the lesson relies on the counter instead.

choices.text: That 15 s hides the cost, and the HOT counter shows it
choices.why: Right: the timing is within noise; 0 HOT updates is not.

prompt: The covering index was 112 MB and `orders_customer_id_idx` 18 MB. About how many times larger is the covering index?
Order the page counts of the December count query as this lesson met them.
trap: The update comes between the clean scan and the dirty one.

prompt: Match each plan line to what it tells you.

pairs.right: every column the query uses is in the index
the visibility map vouched for every page
rows come newest first, but the table is still read
the index did not deliver the order

prompt: Which changes would you expect to make a covering index more expensive to keep? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of HOT and of size.

choices.text: Including a column the application updates after every insert
choices.why: Right: that is total_cents, and it ended HOT updates.

choices.text: Adding a wide text column to INCLUDE
choices.why: Right: every included byte is copied into the index for every row.

choices.text: Moving a rarely updated column from the key to INCLUDE
choices.why: That shrinks the upper levels and changes nothing about HOT.

choices.text: Running VACUUM more often
choices.why: VACUUM keeps the map fresh; it does not add upkeep to the index.
